cim: Keynote speaker at UK Islamophobia conference is former IRGC commander
cim_eredeti: Keynote speaker at UK Islamophobia conference is former IRGC commander
szoveg_eredeti:
Former Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander Saied Reza Ameli, who served as secretary of Iran’s Supreme Council of the Cultural Revolution (SCCR) from 2019 to 2023, an institution involved in developing compulsory hijab policy during the 2019-2022 crackdowns, is to appear as a keynote speaker at a London conference on Islamophobia.

The 13th Islamic Human Rights Commission conference, titled “Artificial Intelligence and Islamophobia,” will be held on December 13. It aims to bring together “leading voices to confront the manifest challenges and implications of AI on Muslims’ lived experiences.”

Ameli is one of three keynote speakers, alongside Shereen Fernandez and Sandew Hira; however, Ameli will be appearing remotely. There will be seven other panelists, some of whom are also controversial figures.

Perhaps most contentious is Open University Senior Lecturer Syed Mustafa Ali, who, in April 2023, shared an article about the murder of Lucy Dee and her two daughters in a Palestinian terrorist attack with the comments: “Dead Zionist settler-colonialists. But they’re white females so we are supposed to grieve for them.”

Alongside him will be Associate UC Berkley professor, Ramón Grosfoguel, who published an essay through IHRC in February 2024 claiming Hamas had not attacked Israeli civilians on October 7. Additionally, Alexandra Darby - AI and Digital Rights Lead at the Forum of European Muslim Youth and Student Organisations (FEMYSO) - will be a panelist. An October 2026 European Parliament resolution identified the FEMYSO as part of the Muslim Brotherhood network.

Iranian human-rights organization Justice for Iran identified Ameli as having served as a deputy brigade commander in the IRGC in the 1980s. Kasra Aarabi, director of IRGC Research at UANI, published a photograph depicting Ameli seated beside Hossein Salami, then-IRGC commander-in-chief.

Ameli spent significant periods studying in both the United States and Britain. He completed high school in the US and has a master’s degree in the sociology of communications from the University College Dublin (UCD) and a doctorate from Royal Holloway, University of London.

After completing his doctorate in 2001, he returned to Iran and subsequently held senior positions in the Islamic Republic’s cultural and cyberspace institutions. He was appointed Fifth Secretary of the Supreme Council of the Cultural Revolution by then-supreme leader Ali Khamenei on January 2, 2019. He held the position until January 17, 2023, serving under consecutive presidents Hassan Rouhani and Ebrahim Raisi.

During Ameli’s four-year tenure, the Supreme Council of the Cultural Revolution – one of Iran’s most powerful ideological policymaking bodies – the Islamic Republic carried out several of its most significant crackdowns on protesters, women, students, and civil society.

The two most notable were the November 2019 protests, during which security forces killed hundreds of demonstrators, and the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom uprising, triggered by the death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini in morality-police custody.

Ameli was personally sanctioned by Canada in February 2023.

The UK subsequently sanctioned the Supreme Council in July 2023 over its role in developing and enforcing mandatory dress codes for women, including policies associated with the use of unreasonable force.

The organization hosting the conference – the UK-based Islamic Human Rights Commission – was co-founded by Ameli himself in 1997. According to the organization National Union for Democracy in Iran (NUFDI), the London-based IHRC positions itself as a nonprofit advocacy entity but has significant ties to the Islamic regime.

An independent government review of the IHRC by Sir William Shawcross referred to it as “an Islamist group ideologically aligned with the Iranian regime that has a history of extremist links and terrorist sympathies.”

IHRC is known for its involvement with pro-Khamenei protests in London, including one in June 2025 where posters were waved bearing the IHRC logo, Khamenei’s face, and the words: “right side of history.”

In May 2025, the Charity Commission watchdog opened an inquiry into IHRC’s charity wing, the Islamic Human Rights Commission Trust, citing “complaints received in relation to the charity’s funding of an event where it is alleged that inflammatory statements were made.”

In October 2025, the Commission announced it was escalating its engagement with the IHRC to a statutory inquiry. On 9 November 2026, the IHRC released a statement claiming the Charity Commission was “pressurizing a popular London venue into cancelling the forthcoming conference on Islamophobia.”

The venue – P21 gallery – reportedly sent an email to IHRC notifying it of the cancellation, citing an emergency meeting with the Charity Commission in which the presence on the speakers’ list of Ameli was discussed. The P21 gallery is itself a charity and a favored venue for pro-Palestine gatherings.

“Prof. Ameli is a prominent Iranian academic, an expert on artificial intelligence, and a global authority on Islamophobia,” the IHRC said, noting that he was to have addressed the conference by video link from Iran.

“It is important to note that Prof. Ameli faces no restrictions or sanctions in the UK and there are no actual accusations of criminality against him. Consequently, there is zero risk of any domestic laws being breached by allowing him to speak.”

IHRC said the annulment of its booking “comes against the backdrop of an increasingly authoritarian attitude being adopted by the Charity Commission in respect of pro-Palestine activities.”

IHRC chair Massoud Shadjareh said, “Despite all the bullying and scandalous attempts to silence us, we will not swerve from telling the truth. The program will go ahead in full, and we will announce a new venue shortly.”

In correspondence with the Daily Mail, the IHRC said that Ameli is “on public record opposing the enforcement of hijab in Iran.”
